Four scenes

◆

Program Analysis

Symbolic Execution

02 June 2026 · Nine minutes

Symbolic execution is a means of analyzing a program to determine what inputs cause each part of it to execute. Instead of running the code on real values, an interpreter walks it while holding every input as a symbol.

It arrives at expressions written in terms of those symbols, and at constraints for the outcome of each conditional branch. Where concrete execution answers what a program does with 5, symbolic execution answers what it would take to reach a place at all.

A worked example

int f() {
  y = read();
  z = y * 2;
  if (z == 12) fail();
}

What makes a vector look drawn

Two things give clip art away, and neither is the drawing. The first is that every edge is mechanically exact; the second is that every fill is perfectly even. The #painted filter fixes the first with a displacement map at scale="3" — small enough that it never reads as a distortion, large enough that no line in the picture is truly straight. Toggle Painted off and the scenes go dead immediately, which is the fastest way to see what it is doing. 

<filter id="painted" x="-10%" y="-10%" width="120%" height="120%">
  <feTurbulence type="fractalNoise" baseFrequency="0.04"
                numOctaves="3" seed="9" result="brush"/>
  <feDisplacementMap in="SourceGraphic" in2="brush" scale="3"
                     xChannelSelector="R" yChannelSelector="G"/>
</filter>

The filter region matters. Displacement pushes pixels outward, so without x="-10%" width="120%" the filter's default region clips the very edges it just moved and the drawing loses its outline.

Placement is most of the work

The kindled world does not get a dark silhouette. Black on white shouts; the scene switches to a sepia wash at roughly a third of the strength, so it sits on the page the way a drawing does rather than sitting on top of it. That is one custom property, not a second drawing.

Below 900px the vignette leaves entirely. It does not fade — a picture at 12% opacity is not a picture, it is a smudge. The text column owns the whole viewport on a phone, and the scene has nowhere to be that is not underneath it.

Each scene spends the gold. Approach has two lit windows, Rest has the bonfire flame, Drowned has one high window. That is the accent already committed, so on those pages the HUD flame is the second and a hovered link is the third — the three-per-viewport ceiling, exactly. Nave spends none: its light shaft is gold at 16% opacity, which is atmosphere rather than accent.

Which page gets which

Approach → home. You are outside, and you have not gone in yet. Seen once per visit, which is the right frequency for the most illustrative of the four.

Nave → listings, posts and tags and archive. You are inside now, and the receding arches are a corridor of entries. The quietest scene, which suits the page you return to most.

Rest → about. A person, sitting down, not going anywhere. It is the only scene with a figure in it, and about is the only page with a person behind it.

Drowned → 404. The tower is ruined, the moon is reflected in water that should not be there, and the reader has arrived somewhere that no longer exists.

Post pages get nothing. Four scenes for four page types works because each is seen occasionally; putting one behind every post would make it wallpaper by the third read, and it would compete with the one thing a post page is for.

Why SVG is the right medium here, not a compromise

It recolours with the world for free. The scenes take fill: currentColor and the parent sets color: var(--scene-ink), so flipping to kindled restyles the drawing rather than swapping a second asset. A pair of PNGs would need two files, two downloads, and a rule to pick between them.

It is a few kilobytes and it never blurs. No image request, no layout shift while it loads, sharp at any zoom or pixel density. On a page whose whole argument is space and light, the vignette should not be the heaviest thing on it.

And the drawing stays editable. The lean of the tower, the height of a spire, whether the figure's head is lower — these are numbers in the path, changeable in a second, which matters because the composition is the part that will actually need iterating.

What to watch. Silhouette is doing all the work, so each scene has to read at a glance in one flat colour — if it needs interior detail to be legible, the shape is wrong and adding lines will not save it. Keep the filters as they are: displacement above about scale="5" stops reading as a brush and starts reading as damage, and a wash mask that dips below roughly 0.6 alpha eats the drawing instead of thinning it.
